1540:
At its most literal, a bastard is a person born to parents who were not married to each other at the time of their birth. The word historically referred to a child considered "illegitimate" — meaning their birth fell outside the boundaries of legal marriage.

For most of human history, being a bastard was not just a label — it came with real consequences. Such a person could not legally inherit their father's title, land, or wealth. They had lower social standing than children born within marriage, and the word carried deep shame. Think of it as a kind of permanent social mark that followed a person their whole life, through no fault of their own.

This is the oldest and most literal sense of the word. Today, it still carries this meaning, but its weight has softened considerably — unmarried parenthood is no longer stigmatized the way it once was, so this specific meaning rarely comes up in everyday speech.
The Much More Common Modern Use: As an Insult

In everyday modern language, bastard is most often used as an insult directed at a person who behaves in a cruel, dishonest, unethical, or deeply unpleasant way.

When someone calls another person a bastard in this sense, they are not commenting on that person's birth parents at all. They are saying:

"This person is contemptible. They acted badly, unfairly, or wickedly."

Examples:

  • "He cheated on her for years and then blamed her for everything. What a bastard."
  • "That bastard stole money from his own employees."
  • "Don't trust him — he's a complete bastard."

The insult ranges in intensity depending on tone and context. At full force, it is a serious, harsh condemnation of someone's character or behavior. It says: this person has no decency.

This is considered a vulgar word — it is not appropriate in formal writing, professional settings, or polite company. However, in casual speech, it is used quite freely, especially in British English.

This is where the word becomes interesting, because bastard can be used in ways that carry zero hostility — and in fact, can express sympathy, affection, or even admiration.

1. The sympathetic "bastard"

When someone says "poor bastard," they are expressing genuine sympathy or pity. There is no insult here.

  • "He lost his job, then his wife left him, and now he's sick. Poor bastard."
  • "She had to work three jobs just to survive. Poor bastard."

The word here almost softens the speaker's tone — it signals that the speaker feels sorry for this person and sees them as a fellow human caught in unfortunate circumstances.

2. The envious "bastard"

When someone says "lucky bastard," they are expressing envy — sometimes playfully, sometimes genuinely.

  • "He won the lottery on his first ticket. Lucky bastard."
  • "She got promoted after just six months. Lucky bastard."

There is no real anger here. It is closer to: "I wish I were in that person's place."

3. The affectionate "bastard" (used between friends)

Among close friends, especially in British and Australian English, the word can be used affectionately — almost as a term of endearment, though a rough one.

  • "You old bastard, I haven't seen you in years! Come here!"
  • "He's a funny bastard, I'll give him that."

This only works when there is genuine warmth and closeness between the speakers. The same words from a stranger would land as a serious insult. Context and relationship are everything here.
For Something Difficult or Unpleasant (Not a Person)

The word can also be applied to things — not people — to describe something that is frustratingly hard, painful, or unpleasant to deal with.

  • "That exam was a real bastard." (It was extremely difficult.)
  • "The last mile of that hike was a total bastard." (It was brutal.)
  • "Getting that screw out was a bastard — it wouldn't budge."

Here the word functions as a way of expressing that something was unexpectedly, frustratingly tough. It has a kind of rueful humor to it.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Because this single word can mean so many different things, the meaning always depends on:

  • Tone of voice: Warm and laughing? Likely affectionate or sympathetic. Cold and contemptuous? It's an insult.
  • The word before it: Poor bastard = sympathy. Lucky bastard = envy. Old bastard = often affectionate. Complete bastard or total bastard = strong insult.
  • Who is speaking to whom: Close friends can use it casually. Between strangers or enemies, it is almost always hostile.
  • What it's describing: If it's a thing (a task, a problem), it means something is very hard or unpleasant.
The Register: When and Where Can You Use It?

• ❌ Formal writing, academic work, professional emails — avoid entirely.
  • ❌ Talking to people you don't know well — it may offend.
  • ✅ Casual conversation among friends — accepted, though still considered a mild expletive.
  • ✅ Reading literature, watching films, understanding dialogue — you'll encounter it frequently.

It is worth knowing that in British and Australian English, this word is used far more casually and frequently than in American English, where it tends to feel slightly more loaded.

Bastard originally meant a child born outside of marriage, and for centuries carried serious social and legal consequences. Today, it is rarely used in that literal sense. Instead, it functions primarily as an insult for a person who behaves cruelly or dishonestly, though it can also express sympathy (poor bastard), envy (lucky bastard), or even rough affection between friends. It can describe something extremely difficult or unpleasant as well. It is a vulgar word, best avoided in formal or polite contexts, but widely used in everyday informal speech — and its exact meaning in any given moment depends almost entirely on tone, context, and the relationship between the speakers.
1541:
When you bastardize something, you take something that was originally good, pure, genuine, or in its proper form — and you corrupt it, weaken it, or degrade it, usually by mixing it with something inferior, changing it carelessly, or stripping away what made it authentic. The result is a version that is worse, less genuine, or distorted compared to the original.

Think of it this way: if you have a beautiful, traditional recipe that has been passed down for generations, and someone comes along and replaces the key ingredients with cheap substitutes and calls it the same dish — they have bastardized that recipe.
The Two Senses of This Word

This word carries two distinct meanings, and you need to know both.

Sense 1 — The Common, Everyday Meaning (Used Most Often Today)

This is the sense you will encounter most frequently in modern speech and writing.

To bastardize something = to corrupt, debase, or degrade it from its original, authentic form — especially by mixing it poorly, simplifying it recklessly, or misrepresenting it.

The key feelings behind this word are:

  • Loss of quality
  • Loss of authenticity
  • A kind of disrespect toward the original

This word is especially used when talking about:

  • Language — when a language is mixed carelessly or degraded
  • Art, music, culture, food, or traditions — when something culturally significant is watered down or distorted
  • Ideas and concepts — when a complex idea is simplified so recklessly that it loses its real meaning

Examples:

  • "Hollywood has completely bastardized this novel. The film keeps the characters' names but throws away everything that made the book meaningful."

Here, the film has distorted the book so badly that it no longer represents what the original work truly was.

  • "Some critics argue that fast-food chains have bastardized Italian cuisine by replacing real ingredients with artificial substitutes just to cut costs."

The food still carries the Italian label, but its authenticity and quality have been destroyed.

  • "The politician bastardized the philosopher's ideas by quoting them out of context and twisting their meaning to serve his own agenda."

The original ideas were genuine and thoughtful; now they have been corrupted into something dishonest.

The emotional weight of this word:

"Bastardize" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong sense of disapproval and criticism. When someone says something has been bastardized, they are expressing that:

  1. The original was worth respecting.
  2. The person or process that changed it did so carelessly or dishonestly.
  3. The result is an inferior, inauthentic shadow of what it once was.

It is a word people use when they feel something valuable has been ruined.

Sense 2 — The Older, Formal/Legal Meaning (Less Common Today)

Historically and in formal/legal contexts, "bastardize" has carried a different and very specific meaning:

To bastardize someone = to officially declare or prove that a person is illegitimate — meaning they were born to parents who were not married to each other, and therefore have no legal right to inherit property, a title, or other privileges.

Example:

  • "The king's enemies sought to bastardize his son in court, hoping to prevent him from inheriting the throne."

In this sense, the word is almost purely a legal or historical term. You might encounter it when reading about monarchy, inheritance law, or historical novels. In everyday modern speech, this sense is rarely used.
The Connection Between the Two Senses

Both senses share the same underlying idea: something is being stripped of its rightful, legitimate status. In the legal sense, a person is declared not legitimate. In the modern sense, a thing — an idea, an art form, a tradition — is made illegitimate by being corrupted. The word travels from the personal to the conceptual, but the core feeling of degradation and loss of genuine status runs through both.

Several other words exist in the same neighborhood — words like corrupt, dilute, distort, dumb down, water down, debase, degrade, adulterate — but "bastardize" combines all of these ideas with an extra layer of meaning: the thing still pretends to be what it was. It still carries the original name or identity, but it has been hollowed out. It is a fake version wearing the costume of the real thing. That is what makes "bastardize" more specific and more powerful than simply saying something was "ruined."

This word is used in both spoken and written language, across formal essays, journalism, literary criticism, cultural commentary, and everyday conversation. It is not a slang word, but it is also not overly academic. It sits comfortably in the middle — usable in a serious editorial, a dinner-table argument about music, or a book review.

It is almost always used in a critical or negative tone. You will rarely, if ever, hear someone use "bastardize" approvingly.

What it meansTo corrupt, degrade, or debase something from its original genuine form — or (historically/formally) to declare a person legally illegitimate
ToneNegative and critical
Used most forCulture, art, language, ideas, traditions, concepts
Key feelingSomething authentic and valuable has been carelessly or dishonestly ruined, yet still claims the original's name
1542: The word baste has two completely different meanings depending on whether you're in a kitchen or working with fabric. It also has a third, older meaning.

To baste means to spoon, brush, or pour liquid over food — usually meat — while it is cooking, especially while it is roasting in an oven or grilling over heat.

The liquid used for basting can be:

  • The meat's own juices that collect at the bottom of the pan
  • Melted butter
  • A marinade, sauce, or broth
  • A mixture of any of these

Why do people baste?
When meat cooks in dry heat (like in an oven), its surface tends to dry out, become tough, and lose flavor. Basting solves this problem. Every time you spoon or brush liquid over the meat, that liquid:

  • Keeps the surface moist so it doesn't dry out or become leathery
  • Adds flavor with every coat of juice or sauce
  • Helps create a beautiful, glossy, golden-brown crust on the outside

How often do you baste?
Typically, you open the oven every 20–30 minutes and spoon the collected pan juices over the meat. Each time you do this, you are basting it.

Example:
"She basted the turkey every half hour so that it would come out juicy and golden."
"He basted the chicken with a mixture of honey, garlic, and butter."

The tool often used for this — a large bulb-shaped tube that sucks up liquid so you can squeeze it over meat — is called a basting syringe or baster. You can also simply use a spoon or a brush.

To baste means to sew pieces of fabric together using long, loose, temporary stitches.

These stitches are not meant to be permanent. They are deliberately made large and easy to remove. The purpose is to hold the fabric in place temporarily — like a pin, but with thread — so you can check the fit, alignment, or shape before you sew the final, permanent stitches.

Think of it as a "draft" stitch — just like you might write a rough draft of something before writing the final version.

Why is basting needed in sewing?

  • Pins can fall out or shift while you're working. Basting stitches hold everything more securely in place.
  • Before committing to permanent stitches on an expensive fabric, a tailor or seamstress baste-stitches first to make sure everything lines up correctly.
  • If something is wrong, you simply pull out the loose basting stitches (because they're long and easy to remove), adjust, and try again — without having damaged the fabric.

These temporary stitches are called basting stitches or sometimes just tacking stitches.

Example:
"She basted the hem before sewing it permanently, just to make sure it was even."
"He basted the two pieces of cloth together so they wouldn't slip under the sewing machine."

In older English and still occasionally in informal use, to baste can mean to hit or beat someone or something — to give someone a good thrashing.

Example:
"The villain threatened to baste him soundly if he didn't hand over the money."

This meaning is quite rare in modern everyday language, so you are far more likely to encounter it in older literature than in modern conversation. You do not need to use it yourself, but it's worth knowing so you're not confused if you come across it.
Quick Summary of All Three Meanings

In the kitchen: Baste = pour or brush liquid repeatedly over cooking food to keep it moist and flavorful.

In sewing: Baste = sew with long, loose, temporary stitches to hold fabric together before the final stitching.

In informal/old language: Baste = to beat or strike someone.

The cooking and sewing meanings are by far the most common and useful ones to know. Both involve a kind of "layering" or "going over" something repeatedly — liquid over meat, or thread over fabric — which is perhaps why the same word ended up covering both.
1543:
A bastion is a stronghold — a place, person, or thing that powerfully protects and preserves something, especially when that something is under threat or disappearing from the world around it.

Think of it this way: imagine a sandcastle being washed away by waves, but one solid, thick corner of it refuses to crumble. That corner is the bastion. It holds firm while everything else gives way.

The word has a literal meaning and a figurative meaning. Both are in active use.

1. The Literal Meaning (Physical/Military)

A bastion is a specific part of an old fort or castle — a thick, raised, outward-jutting structure built into a defensive wall, designed to give soldiers a position from which they could defend the surrounding walls from enemy attack. It was essentially the most heavily reinforced, strategically important section of a fortress. It didn't just protect itself — it helped protect everything else.

So in the physical world, a bastion is:

  • Part of a fortification (a walled defence structure)
  • Built to be especially strong and resistant
  • Positioned to defend and protect something larger

Example sentence: "The soldiers retreated to the bastion when the outer walls were breached."

2. The Figurative Meaning (Everyday Use — FAR More Common)

This is how most people use the word today. When we say something is a bastion, we mean it is a defender or guardian of something — a value, a tradition, a way of life, a belief, a right — especially when that thing is rare, threatened, or fading away in the wider world.

A bastion, in this sense, could be:

  • A place (a city, a country, an institution)
  • An organization (a university, a club, a company)
  • A group of people
  • Even a single person

The key feeling the word carries is: "This is one of the few places/things/people still standing strong for this cause or quality, while the rest of the world has moved away from it."

Example sentences:

  • "The old university was a bastion of free thought." (It fiercely protected the freedom to think and debate, even as other places didn't.)
  • "She was a bastion of integrity in a corrupt industry." (She was the rare, strong exception — someone who held firm to honesty when others around her didn't.)
  • "That small town remains a bastion of traditional culture." (The town has strongly preserved old customs that have vanished elsewhere.)

This is important to understand, because it gives the word its flavour.

"Bastion" is not a neutral word. It carries the feeling of:

  • Strength and resistance — it's not just "a place where X exists," it's "a place that actively stands firm for X."
  • Rarity — calling something a bastion quietly implies that it is one of the few remaining defenders of that thing. If the thing were common and unthreated, you wouldn't use this word.
  • Admiration OR criticism — depending on context, the word can be used approvingly or critically. For example, calling a company "a bastion of innovation" is a compliment. But calling a club "a bastion of outdated prejudice" is a criticism. The word itself is just saying "this place/thing strongly defends X" — whether X is good or bad depends on what's being defended.
The Underlying Logic: Why These Two Meanings Connect

The figurative meaning grew directly from the literal one. A military bastion was the part of a fortress that held its ground and protected what was inside. When people started using the word figuratively, they kept that exact idea: something that holds its ground and protects what it stands for, even under pressure. The image of a fortress wall that won't fall is baked right into the word.

What it isA stronghold; a powerful defender
What it defendsA value, belief, tradition, quality, or right
Key conditionUsually used when that thing is rare, threatened, or disappearing
ToneStrong, firm, resistant — can be admiring or critical
Most common useFigurative (people, places, institutions that defend something)
One Sentence to Remember It By
A bastion is the last strong wall standing — the person, place, or thing that firmly holds up and protects something important, even when the rest of the world no longer does.
1544:
To "not bat an eyelid" means to show absolutely no reaction — no surprise, no shock, no discomfort, and no emotion — even when something unusual, disturbing, or dramatic happens right in front of you.

A person who doesn't bat an eyelid stays completely calm, composed, and unmoved, as if nothing out of the ordinary is happening at all.

Notice the word "not" in that definition. This is important. The idiom is almost always used in the negative form. You will very rarely hear someone say "she batted an eyelid." Instead, you will almost always hear:

  • "She didn't bat an eyelid."
  • "He did it without batting an eyelid."
  • "They never batted an eyelid."
Why an Eyelid? Where Does This Come From?

This is a great question, because understanding the origin will lock the meaning in your memory permanently.

The word "bat" here is not the flying animal. It is a verb that means to flutter or to blink rapidly. It comes from an old French word batre, meaning to beat or to flap.

Now think about what happens to your eyes when you are suddenly surprised or shocked. Your eyelids flutter. You blink. Your eyes widen. These are tiny, automatic physical reactions that your body produces without you even thinking about it. You cannot easily control them. They are a natural signal to the world around you that you have been caught off guard.

So, "batting an eyelid" = the involuntary blinking or fluttering of the eyelid that happens when you are startled or emotionally affected.

Therefore, "not batting an eyelid" = your eyelids don't flutter at all = you show zero physical or emotional reaction. You are so calm, so cool, so in control — or so indifferent — that your body doesn't even flinch.

The idiom is used in everyday conversation and writing. Here are examples across different situations to show you its full range:

Example 1 — Shocking news:
"I told him his flight had been cancelled and he would miss the wedding, but he didn't bat an eyelid. He just calmly booked another one."
Here, the person showed no stress or frustration whatsoever.

Example 2 — An outrageous price:
"The restaurant charged her £500 for dinner, and she paid without batting an eyelid."
Here, she didn't react to the price at all — suggesting it was no big deal to her.

Example 3 — A dangerous or frightening situation:
"The soldier walked through the burning building without batting an eyelid."
Here, it suggests remarkable bravery and calmness under extreme pressure.

Example 4 — Something morally wrong:
"He lied to his entire team and didn't bat an eyelid."
Here, the idiom takes on a darker, more negative tone — he felt no guilt or discomfort about doing something wrong.

Example 5 — An unusual or bizarre event:
"A man walked into the office wearing a full clown costume, and the receptionist didn't bat an eyelid — she'd seen stranger things."
Here, she was so used to unusual events that this one didn't surprise her at all.

This idiom can carry two very different feelings depending on the context, and you must read the situation carefully.

1. Positive or admirable meaning:
Sometimes, not batting an eyelid is a sign of strength, courage, or professionalism. A surgeon who stays calm during a crisis, a pilot who handles an emergency without panicking, a negotiator who doesn't flinch when the other side makes an outrageous demand — these are all positive examples. It means the person has impressive self-control.

2. Negative or cold meaning:
Other times, not batting an eyelid is a sign of callousness, indifference, or cruelty. If someone hears that a friend is suffering and doesn't bat an eyelid, it means they simply don't care. This use of the idiom suggests the person should have reacted but chose not to — or simply felt nothing at all.

The words around the idiom will always tell you which meaning applies.

"Bat an eyelid" is the version most commonly used in British English.

In American English, people more often say "bat an eye" or sometimes "bat an eyelash". All three mean exactly the same thing. If you learn one, you know all three.

  • British: "She didn't bat an eyelid."
  • American: "She didn't bat an eye."
Register — When Should You Use It?

This idiom is informal to neutral. It fits naturally in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends or colleagues
  • Novels, short stories, and journalism
  • Informal essays or blog posts

It would sound slightly out of place in a very formal academic paper or a legal document, but in almost every other setting, it is perfectly appropriate.

Knowing related expressions helps you understand the idiom even more deeply.

  • "Not turn a hair" — very similar; means to remain totally calm and undisturbed.
  • "Not flinch" — to not make any sudden movement of fear or pain; very close in meaning.
  • "Keep a stiff upper lip" — to suppress emotion and stay composed, especially under hardship.
  • "Cool as a cucumber" — completely relaxed and unrattled in a difficult situation.
  • "Unflappable" — an adjective for a person who cannot be made nervous or upset.

All of these share the idea of staying calm and showing no reaction, but "not bat an eyelid" is particularly vivid because it focuses on that tiny, telling flicker of the eye that gives our feelings away — and says: not even that happened.

Core meaningTo show no reaction, surprise, or emotion whatsoever
Almost always used asNegative — "didn't bat an eyelid," "without batting an eyelid"
Origin"Bat" = to flutter; eyelids naturally flutter when we're startled
Can meanBravery/composure OR coldness/indifference, depending on context
British version"Bat an eyelid"
American version"Bat an eye" / "bat an eyelash"

The beauty of this idiom is how physical and human it is. It roots itself in something every single person on earth does involuntarily — blinking in surprise — and then describes someone who doesn't even do that. That image alone should make it impossible to forget.
1545:
A bat mitzvah is a Jewish coming-of-age milestone for girls. The phrase comes from Hebrew and Aramaic and means "daughter of the commandment." In Jewish religious law, a "commandment" (called a mitzvah, plural: mitzvot) is a divine obligation — a rule or duty that Jewish people are expected to follow as part of their faith.

When a Jewish girl reaches a certain age (traditionally 12 years old, though many modern communities use 13), she is considered to have crossed a threshold: she is now spiritually and religiously an adult. From this moment on, she is personally responsible for observing all the mitzvot — the religious duties — that Jewish law places on her. Before this point, that responsibility belonged to her parents. After it, it belongs to her.

So in its most literal, technical sense, a bat mitzvah is the girl herself — she is a "daughter of the commandment," meaning she has become a full moral and religious agent within Judaism. You don't just have a bat mitzvah; strictly speaking, you become one. The phrase describes her new status, not merely an event she attends.

That said, in common usage, the word "bat mitzvah" has also come to refer to the ceremony and celebration that marks this transition — which is how most people use it today.

To understand why this matters so much, you need to understand a little about how Judaism views religious obligation.

In Jewish law, every Jewish person above a certain age is bound by a set of commandments — rules about prayer, food, observance of holy days, ethical behavior, and much more. A child is not yet fully bound by these. But once a girl turns 12 (or a boy turns 13, as discussed below), she or he is now fully accountable before God for fulfilling these obligations.

This is not just a symbolic gesture. It means the young person can now:

  • Be counted as a full adult member of the Jewish community in religious contexts
  • Be called to read from the Torah (the Jewish holy scripture) publicly during worship
  • Lead certain prayers and religious rituals (in many denominations)
  • Sign religious legal documents
  • Take on the full weight of Jewish religious life independently

The bat mitzvah moment is therefore not just a party. It is a legal and spiritual transformation in the eyes of Jewish religious law.

The bat mitzvah ceremony is typically held at a synagogue (a Jewish house of worship), most often on a Saturday morning, which is the Jewish Sabbath — the holiest day of the week and the most important time for communal worship and Torah reading.

During the ceremony, the bat mitzvah girl (the one being honored) typically:

  • Reads aloud from the Torah scroll — a handwritten parchment scroll containing the Five Books of Moses. The reading is in Hebrew, chanted according to a traditional melodic system. Each week, a specific portion (parasha) of the Torah is read, and the bat mitzvah will read (or chant) from that week's assigned portion.
  • Reads from the Haftarah — a related passage from the Prophets section of the Hebrew Bible, also chanted in Hebrew.
  • Delivers a speech (called a d'var Torah, meaning "word of Torah") — a short talk in which she discusses the meaning or lesson of the Torah portion she read, often connecting it to her own life or values.

This demonstrates that she has studied Hebrew, learned to read sacred texts, and can now participate as a full adult in Jewish worship.

A bat mitzvah is not something a girl simply shows up to. It typically requires years of preparation, including:

  • Attending Hebrew school to learn the Hebrew language and Jewish religious traditions
  • Learning to read from the Torah, which is written without vowels or musical notations and must be chanted correctly from memory or close study
  • Studying her specific Torah portion in depth
  • Working with a rabbi (a Jewish religious leader) or a tutor

This preparation itself is considered a crucial part of the process — it is the education that makes her ready to take on adult religious responsibility.

Following the religious ceremony, it is customary to hold a celebratory gathering — often a party or reception — with family and friends. In many communities, especially in the United States, these celebrations have grown into elaborate, joyful events with food, music, dancing, and gifts.

It is important to note, however, that the party is a cultural tradition layered on top of the ceremony — it is not what makes someone a bat mitzvah. The religious status is conferred by the age and the Jewish community's recognition of it, with or without a ceremony or party. Even a girl who never has any formal ceremony at all still becomes a bat mitzvah at age 12 simply by reaching that age — the ceremony is a public, communal celebration of something that happens regardless.
How it differs from a bar mitzvah

The male equivalent is called a bar mitzvah — "son of the commandment." The age for boys is 13 (not 12 like girls). The structure of the ceremony is essentially the same.

Historically, the bar mitzvah has existed as a formal ceremony for centuries. The bat mitzvah ceremony for girls is much newer — the first recorded formal bat mitzvah ceremony in the modern sense was held in 1922 in New York, for a rabbi's daughter. Before that, girls' coming-of-age was acknowledged quietly or not at all in most Jewish communities, even though the legal status still applied to them.

Today, whether and how a bat mitzvah ceremony is conducted varies significantly across different branches of Judaism:

  • Orthodox Judaism tends to have more limited or separate ceremonies for girls, often not including public Torah reading by women, due to traditional interpretations of religious law.
  • Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, and other liberal denominations generally conduct bat mitzvah ceremonies that are nearly identical in scope and format to bar mitzvah ceremonies.

When referring to multiple people or events, the word takes a Hebrew plural form. Multiple girls who have become bat mitzvah are called b'not mitzvah (daughters of the commandment). Together, boys and girls who have come of age are called b'nei mitzvah (children of the commandment). In casual English, people often just say "bat mitzvahs" when referring to multiple ceremonies.

A bat mitzvah is, at once, a person (a Jewish girl who has crossed the threshold into religious adulthood at age 12), a legal and spiritual status (the responsibility for fulfilling the Jewish commandments now rests on her, not her parents), and a ceremony (a public, communal celebration — usually at a synagogue on Saturday — where she reads from the Torah and is recognized as a full adult member of the Jewish faith). It represents one of the most meaningful milestones in a Jewish girl's life, marking the moment she steps fully into the religious tradition she was raised in and takes ownership of it for herself.
1546:
A batch is a group of things of the same kind that are made, collected, or handled together, at one time.

The key thought behind this word is: instead of doing things one by one, you do them as a group, all at once. That group is a batch.

Three things are always true about a batch:

1. The items are similar or of the same type.
You make a batch of cookies — not a batch of cookies and a random chair thrown in. The things in a batch belong together because they're the same kind of thing.

2. They are grouped together deliberately.
A batch isn't a random pile. Someone consciously decides: "These things go together." They are collected or produced as one defined set.

3. They are made or dealt with together, in one go.
This is the heart of the word. The items in a batch share the same "session" — the same baking session, the same production run, the same processing moment.

Imagine a baker. She puts 12 cookies in the oven at 9 AM. Those 12 cookies come out together. That is one batch. Then at 10 AM, she puts another 12 cookies in. That is a second batch.

Notice: she didn't bake 24 cookies all at once. She baked them in batches — one group at a time. This is the most natural, intuitive example of the word.

The word travels across many areas of life, always carrying the same core meaning:

In cooking and baking:
"I made three batches of muffins for the party." Each time you bake a set of muffins, that's one batch.

In manufacturing and production:
Factories make products in batches. A pharmaceutical company might manufacture 10,000 bottles of medicine together in one production run — that is one batch. If something goes wrong, they can trace exactly which batch was affected (this is why medicine bottles have a "batch number" on them).

In computing:
A "batch" of data or tasks means a set of items that are processed together by a computer in one operation, rather than one at a time or in real time. For example, a bank might process all of the day's transactions at midnight in one batch, rather than updating your account every single second.

In everyday life:
The word is used loosely and naturally for any group of similar things that arrive or are dealt with together:

  • "A batch of emails" — a bunch of emails that came in together.
  • "A batch of new students" — a group of students who joined the school at the same time.
  • "A batch of applications" — a set of job applications received in the same period.
  • "A fresh batch of problems" — a new set of issues to solve.
A Subtle But Important Quality: Batches Imply Repetition

When someone says "a batch," they naturally suggest that there are, or could be, other batches. It's not just one single, unique group — it's one of potentially many rounds.

This is different from saying "a group" or "a collection," which don't carry that sense of repetition. "A batch" tells you: this is one round of something that happens in rounds.

A batch can be tiny or enormous. A batch of two cookies is still a batch. A batch of a million car parts is still a batch. What matters is not how big the group is, but the fact that the items were made or handled together, as one defined set.

• "a fresh batch" — a newly made or newly arrived group. "There's a fresh batch of bread at the bakery."
  • "in batches" — doing something group by group rather than all at once. "We'll process the orders in batches."
  • "a batch of" — the standard way to use the word, followed by whatever the items are. "A batch of reports."
  • "batch number" — an identification number assigned to a particular batch during production, used for tracking.
  • "the first/second/next batch" — specifying which round or group you mean.
A batch is a defined group of similar things that are produced, processed, or handled together, in one session — one of potentially many such rounds.
1547: "Bate" is a word with several distinct meanings, depending on the context in which it is used. Each meaning belongs to a different world — one to everyday language, one to the world of birds, one to leathermaking, and one to British slang.
Meaning 1: To Hold Back, Reduce, or Restrain Something

This is the core and most important meaning of "bate." When you bate something, you hold it back, tone it down, or reduce its strength or intensity. You are keeping something from going at full force.

Think of it like turning down a dial — not switching something off, but making it quieter, weaker, or less intense.

Examples:

  • A nervous student waiting outside the exam hall waits with bated breath — meaning they are holding their breath, almost afraid to breathe, out of suspense or excitement. Their breathing is restrained, pulled back.
  • A judge might bate the strictness of a punishment — meaning they soften it, reduce it.
  • "He could not bate his excitement as the results were announced." — He could not hold his excitement back.

"With bated breath" is by far the most common place you will encounter this meaning of the word. If you've ever read or heard someone say "everyone waited with bated breath," now you know exactly what it means: with breath held back, tightly restrained — the physical thing a person does when they are tense, anxious, or deeply eager.
Meaning 2: To Beat the Wings Wildly (Falconry)

In the world of falconry — the ancient practice of training birds of prey like hawks and falcons to hunt — "bate" has a very specific meaning.

When a hawk bates, it beats its wings frantically and tries to fly off the falconer's gloved fist or its perch, but it is held back by its jesses (the leather straps attached to its legs). The bird panics, flutters violently, and hangs mid-air for a moment before being settled back down.

A hawk might bate out of fear, excitement, or agitation. It is an involuntary, impulsive reaction — the bird cannot control itself. A well-trained hawk bates less and less over time.

Example:

  • "The young falcon bated every time a stranger came near." — It flapped and lurched off the perch in fear.
Meaning 3: To Soak and Soften Hides (Leathermaking / Tanning)

In the craft of tanning — turning raw animal hides into leather — "bate" refers to a specific step in the process.

After the hair is removed from a hide, the skin is still stiff and harsh. To soften it and make it workable, tanners bate the hide by soaking it in a special alkaline liquid or solution containing enzymes. This breaks down unwanted proteins and relaxes the fibres of the skin, making it soft, supple, and ready for the next step of tanning.

So when you bate a hide, you are essentially treating it with a softening bath.

Example:

  • "The skins were bated overnight in a warm solution before tanning could begin."
Meaning 4: To Be in a Rage (British Informal)

In informal British English — particularly in older usage and in certain regional dialects — if someone is bating, they are in a furious temper. "A bate" (used as a noun here too) means a fit of rage or a bad mood.

Examples:

  • "Don't bate at me — it wasn't my fault!" — Don't rage at me.
  • "He came home in a right bate." — He came home absolutely furious. (noun form, but worth knowing alongside the verb)

This meaning is not used widely in modern, formal, or international English, but you may come across it in British literature or conversation.

This is an old and now largely obsolete meaning. In earlier English, to bate something from a sum meant to take it away or deduct it.

Example:

  • "Bate a few pence from the price, and we have a deal." — Subtract a few pence.

You are unlikely to encounter this meaning in modern writing except in very old texts or historical novels.
A Quick Summary of All the Meanings

• Restrain / reduce / hold back → "with bated breath" (most common and important)
  • A hawk fluttering wildly off a perch → falconry term
  • Soften a hide in tanning solution → leathermaking
  • Be in a furious rage → British informal
  • Deduct or subtract → archaic, rarely used today
The One You Must Know Cold

Of all these meanings, "bate" meaning to hold back or restrain is the one that matters most to you as a learner, because it lives on in the phrase "with bated breath" — which is extremely common in literature, journalism, and everyday speech. Now that you know what "bate" truly means, that phrase will never be a mystery to you again. You will read it and instantly understand: someone is holding back even their very breath — so tense, so eager, so gripped by anticipation that they can barely breathe.
1548:
Bathetic describes something that creates a jarring, deflating feeling — either because it suddenly drops from something grand and serious down to something trivial and silly, or because it is dripping with so much forced, fake emotion that it feels cheap and manipulative rather than genuinely moving.

It is the adjective form of the noun bathos. Think of bathos as the opposite of the feeling you get when something lives up to its dramatic buildup. Bathos is what happens when that buildup collapses — either into absurdity, or into hollow tearjerking.

There are two flavors of bathetic, and both matter.

This is the most classic use. Something is bathetic when it starts at a high, serious, or grand level — and then crashes down without warning into something embarrassingly small or mundane.

Think of it this way: imagine someone building a magnificent cathedral, brick by brick, floor by floor, reaching the sky — and then placing a plastic garden gnome on top as the final touch. That gnome is bathetic. It doesn't belong. It kills the grandeur instantly.

Example in writing:

"He had survived two world wars, escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp, and crossed three continents on foot. Last Thursday, he slipped on a banana peel."

The last sentence is bathetic. The list builds and builds — war, escape, heroism — and then collapses into slapstick. The crash is so sudden and so steep that it is almost funny. That collision between the grand and the ridiculous is exactly what bathetic means in this sense.

This is why bathetic writing often has an unintentionally comic effect, even when the writer intended to be serious. If you write a solemn, heartbreaking eulogy and accidentally end it with a trivial sentence, the result is bathetic — and the audience might laugh or cringe at exactly the wrong moment.

Another example:

"The storm was apocalyptic. Lightning split the sky. Thunder shook the earth. She worried she might get her hair wet."

The last line is bathetic. It yanks you from the dramatic storm down to a petty vanity, and the tonal collision is jarring.
Flavor 2: Fake or Overdone Emotion (False Sentimentality)

The second meaning is slightly different. Here, something is bathetic not because of an abrupt tonal drop, but because it is wallowing in emotion so heavily and so artificially that it stops feeling real and starts feeling manipulative or embarrassing.

Think of a TV commercial that uses slow piano music, a child with wide tearful eyes, and soft golden lighting — all to sell you a brand of paper towels. The emotion is performed, not earned. It is designed to squeeze a feeling out of you through sheer manipulation, not through anything genuinely moving. That is bathetic.

Or think of a soap opera scene where a character weeps dramatically and delivers a ten-minute monologue about a problem that most people would handle with a phone call. The emotion is so exaggerated, so much more than the situation warrants, that it tips over into something cringeworthy. That is also bathetic.

In this sense, bathetic overlaps with words like maudlin (weepily sentimental) or saccharine (sickeningly sweet), but bathetic carries the specific idea that the emotion fails — it tries to move you but instead makes you roll your eyes, or feel vaguely manipulated.

A useful way to think about it: Genuine pathos (real, earned emotion) makes you feel. Bathetic emotion makes you aware that you are being made to feel — and that awareness kills the effect. The curtain gets pulled back, and you see the machinery.

This is an important distinction that many people miss.

Unintentional bathos is a writing flaw. The writer wanted to be solemn, grand, or deeply moving — but the result is deflating or hollow. This is the kind that makes readers cringe or snicker at a funeral scene.

Intentional bathos is a literary device — and a powerful one. Writers, comedians, and poets use it deliberately to create comic effect, to deflate pomposity, or to mock something by treating it with absurdly mismatched grandeur. Alexander Pope, one of history's most celebrated poets, built an entire famous poem (The Rape of the Lock) on intentional bathos — he used the full, epic, heroic style of ancient war poetry to describe a petty social squabble over a stolen lock of hair. The joke works because the mismatch between style and subject is so bathetic.

So when you call something bathetic, context tells you whether it is a failure or a carefully aimed joke.

Because the two words sound so similar, people confuse them constantly — but they mean completely different things.

Pathetic (from pathos) means either arousing pity and sadness, or — in everyday informal use — pitifully inadequate ("that excuse is pathetic").

Bathetic (from bathos) means characterized by an anticlimactic crash from the grand to the trivial, or by false/overdone sentimentality.

The connection between them is that bathos is essentially what happens when an attempt at genuine pathos goes wrong — when emotion is so overdone or so poorly placed that it collapses. But the two words are not interchangeable.

A person crying at a funeral is pathetic (in the classical, sympathetic sense). A funeral speech that starts with profound words about life and death and ends with a joke about the deceased's bad parking habits is bathetic. A movie that makes you cry is pathetic (in the best sense). A movie that tries too hard to make you cry by piling on obvious emotional triggers until you feel manipulated is bathetic.

You would call something bathetic when:

  • A piece of writing, speech, or performance drops abruptly from a high tone to a trivial one in a way that is deflating or unintentionally comic.
  • A story, film, advertisement, or performance lays emotion on so thick and so artificially that it feels hollow, cloying, or manipulative rather than genuinely touching.

Example sentences:

  • "The speech was supposed to be moving, but the bathetic ending — a joke about his cat — left the audience confused."
  • "The film's final act was so bathetic, so relentlessly tearful and manipulative, that I felt annoyed rather than sad."
  • "It is a bathetic image: a warrior in full armour, weeping over a broken biscuit."

If you ever need to remember what bathetic means: it describes the awkward, deflating, or manipulative failure that happens when something reaches for grandeur or genuine feeling — and instead lands with a thud.
1549:
Bathos is the jarring, often humorous effect created when something grand, serious, or emotionally weighty is suddenly undercut by something trivial, silly, or absurdly mundane. Think of it as a steep drop in dignity — you're climbing a staircase of importance and gravitas, and then, without warning, you fall face-first into a puddle.

The word has two closely related meanings, and understanding both is essential.
The first meaning: an abrupt plunge from the grand to the trivial

This is the most common meaning. It happens when writing, speech, or film builds up something solemn and important — and then immediately deflates it with something petty or absurd. The gap between the two levels is where bathos lives.

Here's a clear example: "She had survived heartbreak, poverty, and the collapse of an entire empire — and then she lost her keys."

Notice how the sentence opens with enormous weight — heartbreak, poverty, the fall of empires — and then suddenly lands on losing keys. That drop, from the colossal to the petty, is bathos. The reader expects the sentence to end somewhere worthy of what came before, and instead it falls off a cliff into the ordinary.

Now, this kind of bathos can be either intentional or unintentional, and the difference matters enormously.

Intentional bathos is a deliberate technique. Skilled writers use it as a tool for comedy, satire, or to gently puncture something that's being too pompous or overblown. When done well, it's genuinely funny — the drop is the joke. Alexander Pope, the 18th-century poet, was a master of this. In The Rape of the Lock, he wrote about a woman having a lock of her hair stolen as though it were an earth-shattering, epic-scale tragedy — full of grand, heroic language — and the entire joke rests on the absurd contrast between the weightiness of the writing and the triviality of the event. He was skewering vanity by using bathos as a scalpel.

Unintentional bathos is the opposite: a writer tries sincerely to be moving or majestic, but accidentally slips into the ridiculous. This is a flaw, not a technique. Imagine a poem that builds toward a devastating emotional peak and then concludes: "O Death, thou conqueror of all — / The brave, the noble, the great, / And Mike from Accounts, who tripped on a ball." The writer probably meant for that last line to feel humanizing and touching. Instead, the casual, mundane detail kills the mood stone dead. The poem tried to be a cathedral and became a garden shed.
The second meaning: excessive, overdone, or fake emotion

The second meaning of bathos is sentimentality taken so far that it collapses into hollowness or even unintentional comedy — emotion that is so exaggerated, so relentlessly laid on, that it stops feeling genuine and starts feeling manipulative or absurd.

Picture a film where every single scene has someone weeping in slow motion, with swelling orchestral music playing underneath, whether the moment earns it or not. After a while, all that heaped-on emotion starts to feel not moving, but exhausting — and eventually laughable. That is bathos. The film was reaching for your heartstrings so desperately and so clumsily that it missed them entirely.

Here, bathos isn't about a sudden drop in tone, but about a collapse under the weight of too much emotion. When you try too hard to make something moving, it stops being moving. It becomes soggy. Genuine pathos (see below) earns its emotion; bathos in this sense begs for it and makes you want to back away.

They share a common thread: in both cases, something fails to achieve the effect it was aiming for — or achieves a deliberately comic version of failure. The first meaning fails by going too low after going high (the sudden drop). The second meaning fails by going too high for too long (the emotional overload). In both cases, the result is a feeling of deflation — either sudden, like a needle popping a balloon, or gradual, like a balloon quietly going flat over days. The key concept in both is a fall from what is elevated.

These two words look nearly identical and are frequently confused, so it's worth being precise. Pathos is genuine, skillfully evoked emotion — the quality in a piece of writing or art that makes you feel something real, because the emotion has been honestly earned. Think of a scene in a novel that makes you cry, not because the writer forced it, but because they built it carefully and truthfully. That's pathos working as it should.

Bathos is what goes wrong: either it's the fake, manufactured version of pathos (the second meaning — overdone emotion that rings hollow), or it's the sudden drop that kills real emotion by introducing something trivial (the first meaning). Pathos elevates; bathos deflates. Pathos trusts the reader; the bathetic kind of excess manipulates them, and the tonal-drop kind blindsides them with the mundane.

These are close relatives but not the same thing. An anticlimax is any disappointing ending or letdown — a story builds and builds, and then fizzles out weakly. Bathos is more specific: it requires that distinct gap in register between the grand and the trivial, and the drop from one to the other. All bathos involves anticlimax, but not all anticlimaxes are bathos. If a thriller novel spends 400 pages building toward a confrontation between hero and villain, and then the villain simply gives up and goes home, that's anticlimactic — flat and disappointing. But if the hero defeats the villain in an epic battle and then immediately trips over his shoelace and falls into a bin, that's bathetic — the gap between the epic and the absurd is right there, and it produces that characteristic drop.

When you want to describe something as exhibiting bathos, the adjective is bathetic. A badly written tragedy might be called bathetic. An overwrought film score might be described as bathetic. An overly dramatic political speech that ends with something embarrassingly small might land bathetically.

Bathos is the effect — comic, cringeworthy, or simply deflating — produced when something solemn or grand is suddenly undercut by the trivial, or when emotion is piled on so excessively that it becomes hollow. It can be deployed on purpose as one of literature's sharpest comic tools, or it can arrive accidentally as a mark of poor craft and misjudgment. Either way, it is always about a fall — from what is high to what is low, from what is genuine to what is overwrought.

Once you know this word, you'll start noticing it everywhere: in clumsy newspaper headlines, in overwrought film scores, in political speeches that reach for greatness and land on a typo — and in the hands of the best satirists who ever lived, who used that fall not as a failure but as a perfectly aimed arrow.
